candidate_concepts.label: Monte Carlo Simulation for Investment Risk Assessment
candidate_concepts.description: The Monte Carlo method stochastically models risk factors to generate a full probability distribution of a financial criterion (e.g., profit), enabling comprehensive risk assessment beyond deterministic point estimates.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the steps of Monte Carlo simulation: define risk factors with probability distributions, run thousands of iterations, and interpret a frequency histogram of outcomes.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article explicitly presents Monte Carlo simulation as the core of its methodology (Sections 3.3 and 4) and demonstrates its application with Crystal Ball on two projects, generating profit distributions.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is a single, well-defined method that can be taught as a standalone risk assessment technique.

candidate_concepts.source_name: New Approaches to Project Risk Assessment Utilizing the Monte Carlo Method

candidate_concepts.label: Sensitivity Analysis to Identify Key Risk Factors
candidate_concepts.description: Sensitivity analysis using tornado graphs and spider charts rank risk factors by their impact on the criterion value, helping prioritize which variables to focus on in risk management.
coverage_criteria: Student can interpret a tornado graph: identify the factor with the widest bar, explain quantile ranges, and determine direction of impact.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 3.2 describes sensitivity analysis via tornado graphs and spider charts as part of the simulation environment, and Figures 4-7 provide visual examples.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific analytical tool within Monte Carlo simulation, appropriate for a focused lesson on interpreting model outputs.

candidate_concepts.label: Risk Mapping for Preliminary Risk Identification
candidate_concepts.description: Risk mapping involves expert assessment of probability and impact to create a matrix that categorizes risks as acceptable, temporarily acceptable, or unacceptable, guiding quantitative analysis.
coverage_criteria: Student can create a risk matrix given a list of risks, assign probability and impact scores, and explain how the matrix informs subsequent simulation focus.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 3.1 presents risk mapping with a risk matrix (Figure 3) and explains how it led to selecting financial risks for the Monte Carlo simulation.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Risk mapping is a distinct step before simulation, teachable as a separate qualitative technique.

candidate_concepts.source_name: New Approaches to Project Risk Assessment Utilizing the Monte Carlo Method

candidate_concepts.label: Comparing Projects with Probabilistic Decision Criteria
candidate_concepts.description: When choosing between projects with simulation results, use statistical indicators (mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation) and rules like preferring projects with higher mean and lower standard deviation, or the lower coefficient of variation when means differ.
coverage_criteria: Student can compare two projects using mean, standard deviation, and skewness; identify which project is preferable based on given decision rules; and explain the coefficient of variation trade-off.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 4 explicitly lists decision criteria for comparing two projects based on simulation statistics (Table 2), and applies them to select the A project.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept encapsulates the actionable decision-making step that translates simulation outputs into a clear recommendation.

candidate_concepts.label: Deterministic vs. Stochastic Approaches to Risk Assessment
candidate_concepts.description: Deterministic models use single most-likely values, while stochastic models incorporate uncertainty through probability distributions, providing a more complete picture of risk and enabling probabilistic decisions.
coverage_criteria: Student can contrast deterministic and stochastic modeling with examples, and explain why stochastic methods are preferred for risk assessment.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The introduction (Section 1) distinguishes deterministic and stochastic approaches, and the article positions Monte Carlo as a superior stochastic method for investment decisions.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This foundational comparison sets the stage for understanding the need for Monte Carlo simulation, making it a teachable concept of appropriate scope.

candidate_concepts.label: Crystal Ball Software for Monte Carlo Simulation
candidate_concepts.description: Crystal Ball is an Excel add-in that facilitates Monte Carlo simulation by generating random numbers, performing sensitivity analysis, and producing graphical outputs like tornado charts and probability distributions.
coverage_criteria: Student can list key features of Crystal Ball and explain how it simplifies running simulations and sensitivity analyses for non-experts.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article uses Crystal Ball throughout the methodology (Sections 2, 3) and explicitly discusses its role and sensitivity calculation method.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: As a specific tool mentioned, this is a concrete element that students might encounter in practice.

source_local_connector_candidates.reason: The article describes how risk mapping (Section 3.1) was used to identify that financial risks are the highest, leading to the decision to set profit as the criterion value in the Monte Carlo simulation (Section 3.3).

The article uses the statistical outputs of the Monte Carlo simulation (Table 2) to apply decision rules in Section 4, resulting in the recommendation to choose the A project as less risky and more advantageous.
